pilot.head()

pilot.describe(include='all')


plt.figure(figsize=(9,4))
sns.lineplot(data=pilot, x='timestamp', y='occupancy_count', hue='condition')
plt.title('Occupancy over time (pilot)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Mean dwell time by condition with 95% CIs.

_ = plot_error_bars(pilot, group_col='condition', value_col='dwell_time_mean_min', title='Dwell time (mean ± 95% CI)')
plt.show()



Independent t-test on dwell time between A and B (pilot scale).

a = pilot.loc[pilot.condition=='A', 'dwell_time_mean_min']
b = pilot.loc[pilot.condition=='B', 'dwell_time_mean_min']
stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)





Box/violin charts communicate variability quickly.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(10,4))
sns.boxplot(data=pilot, x='condition', y='occupancy_count', ax=ax[0])
sns.violinplot(data=pilot, x='condition', y='dwell_time_mean_min', ax=ax[1])
ax[0].set_title('Occupancy distribution')
ax[1].set_title('Dwell time distribution')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()




Resample with replacement to estimate uncertainty without heavy math.

def bootstrap_ci(x, n_boot=2000, ci=0.95, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        sample = rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True)
        means.append(np.mean(sample))
    lo = np.percentile(means, (1-ci)/2*100)
    hi = np.percentile(means, (1+(ci))/2*100)
    return float(np.mean(means)), float(lo), float(hi)

for cond in ['A','B']:
    m, lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(pilot.loc[pilot.condition==cond, 'dwell_time_mean_min'].values)
    print(cond, 'mean≈', round(m,2), 'CI', (round(lo,2), round(hi,2)))

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
What you’ll learn

In plain language A clear mental model of how ML works without math overload — and where it helps (and where it doesn’t) in architectural workflows.


the 12 principles that make ML predictable, not mysterious
how to use generative tools responsibly for studio work
everything reproducible: prompts, seeds, masks, versions


This is the skinned summary. The full detailed deck — pipeline, diffusion, segmentation, surrogate modeling, GH/Honeybee tooling — is the original ML for Architecture PDF.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
How to read each principle
Every principle uses the same four-part frame — the same shape as the course’s own evidence logic:


Idea the principle itself


Why it matters what it changes for you




Studio example how it shows up in design


Quick activity · 2 min apply it to your project

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules
text:
Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules

Idea An ML model is a function f(x) → y whose parameters are fit from examples (x, y).



Why it matters Expect pattern recognition, not hand-coded logic. The model learns regularities present in the data.


Studio example (massing image) → predicted daylight metric; (facade photo) → style label.



Quick activity · 2 min Name three inputs you could give a model in your current studio project. What output would you want?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 2 — Data is the design brief
text:
Principle 2 — Data is the design brief

Idea The dataset defines what the model can and cannot learn.



Why it matters Better data beats fancier models — curate for coverage and quality, not just quantity.


Studio example A facade-style classifier fails if trained only on one region or era.



Quick activity · 2 min List two gaps in a “facade” dataset that would cause failures on your campus. How would you fill them?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned
text:
Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned

Idea How we encode inputs (pixels, meshes, graphs, text) determines what the model can “see”.



Why it matters Choosing a representation is like selecting a drawing type: plan vs section vs perspective.


Studio example Street photos (pixels) for segmentation vs adjacency graphs for layout optimization.



Quick activity · 2 min For your task, would pixels, vectors, meshes, or text be best — and why?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 4 — Loss = what “better” means

Idea The loss function translates “good” into math; models only improve on what loss rewards.



Why it matters If the loss ignores safety or legibility, the model will too. This is your threshold, made explicit.


Studio example A daylight surrogate with MSE learns averages; worst-case glare needs a different objective.



Quick activity · 2 min Write a one-line “loss” for your project (e.g., minimize peak glare while keeping daylight autonomy above target).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 5 — Training = reduce loss (gradient descent)

Idea Training iteratively adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces loss.



Why it matters Explains learning rate, convergence, and why training looks rough before it stabilizes.


Studio example Don’t judge early iterations; monitor the validation curve, not the first guesses.



Quick activity · 2 min Sketch how you’d know training is “done” (hint: validation loss / early stopping).

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 6 — Generalization is the goal

Idea We care about performance on new, unseen data — not just the training set.



Why it matters Overfitting = memorization; good models transfer to the next site or city.


Studio example A roof-type detector perfect on your curated set fails on cloudy days.



Quick activity · 2 min Name two differences between training images and deployment images. How will you test generalization?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific
text:
Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific

Idea Underfit models are too simple; overfit models memorize noise.



Why it matters You control this via model capacity, augmentation, and regularization.


Studio example A tiny model misses brick vs terracotta; a huge model memorizes specific buildings.



Quick activity · 2 min Which knob would you turn first to reduce overfit — augmentation, regularization, or more data?

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions
text:
Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions

Idea Predictions are probabilistic; confidence varies by context and input quality.



Why it matters This is the course thesis in ML form: sample multiple outputs and critique; avoid single-image “truth”.


Studio example Use seeds and A/B comparisons for renders, not one lucky frame.



Quick activity · 2 min Generate 3 variations (same seed + small prompt tweaks); choose and justify one.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 9 — Distribution shift breaks models

Idea When deployment data differ from training (climate, culture, camera), expect failure.



Why it matters Plan pilots on real sites; monitor drift; retrain when needed.


Studio example A Berlin-trained segmenter struggles in Bangkok (materials, colors, sky).



Quick activity · 2 min Write one “shift” you expect in your project and a way to detect it.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 10 — Generative models = distributions + conditioning

Idea Diffusion models learn a distribution and sample from it; prompts/masks/refs condition the sampling.



Why it matters Prompts steer; seeds give reproducibility; masks and references preserve geometry and identity.


Studio example Keep geometry via masks; change cladding via prompt; reuse the same seed for versions.



Quick activity · 2 min Take a white-model view; list what you’d mask vs what you’d let the model change.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
section: Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task
text:
Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task

Idea Pick metrics that reflect the goal and pair them with human A/B judgment for visuals.



Why it matters Numbers alone can reward “pretty wrong” results.


Studio example For concept imagery, use pairwise preference + a rubric (material legibility, camera plausibility).



Quick activity · 2 min Draft two rubric criteria to compare two generated facade images.

title: ML Primer: The 12 Principles
text:
Principle 12 — Ethics, IP, and human-in-the-loop

Idea Datasets carry bias; licenses and privacy matter; designers remain accountable.



Why it matters You choose sources, cite them, disclose process, and keep clients safe.


Studio example Use open/owned references; document prompts, seeds, masks; avoid identifying people without consent.



Quick activity · 2 min Pick one slide of your own and add a visible credit line for every image source.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
text:
If you can’t rerun it, it isn’t evidence
A result becomes evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it — and ideally reproduce it.

The week’s question If you left the project tomorrow, could someone trust your output without you in the room to explain it?

Documentation is not paperwork after the fact. It is the part of the method that makes the output legible.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
text:
Where reproducibility quietly fails
These are ordinary, not dramatic — and they happen to careful people.







Failure
What was lost




Plugin / version not recorded
the file won’t reopen or rerun later


Settings changed but not noted
results can’t be matched to inputs


One person held the knowledge
nobody else can defend the method


CRS / units left implicit
spatial output is silently wrong


AI output treated as final evidence
a claim no one actually checked




The risk is not embarrassment. It is presenting a result you can no longer stand behind.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: When the spreadsheet silently rewrote the data
text:
When the spreadsheet silently rewrote the data

What happened Geneticists found that Excel was auto-converting gene names into dates and numbers (for example “SEPT2” became a date). A 2016 study found errors in roughly one in five papers with supplementary spreadsheets — the field eventually renamed the genes rather than fight the software.


The lesson Reproducibility starts with knowing what your tool did to your data. Document formats, versions, and import settings — the failure is invisible until someone re-runs it.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
text:
A quick, honest poll
Have you ever struggled to reconstruct what you did on a project from a few months ago?

Almost everyone has. The point is not guilt — it is to treat documentation as a normal, expected part of the workflow, starting with one process today.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Document one workflow so it stands alone
text:
Document one workflow so it stands alone
Pick the most complex or critical workflow in your project — the one you would least want to lose.

Do this now · 10 minutes Write step-by-step instructions clear enough that a classmate who has never seen your method could follow them and get your result — with no verbal explanation from you.

Candidates: a Grasshopper setup, a survey-data analysis, a GIS operation, a Python notebook, a statistical step.

The documentation swap
We test documentation the only honest way: someone else follows it cold.


Exchange · 2 min Swap with someone whose method differs from yours. No verbal notes — the instructions must stand alone.


Attempt · 8 min Follow their steps exactly. Mark where you get confused, stuck, or have to guess.


Feedback · 5 min Report what was unclear, what was missing, and the one change that would help most.



The gaps you find are the gaps a future reader would hit. This is the most useful feedback you will get all week.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: What large models are, for this course
text:
What large models are, for this course

The short version Large models are probabilistic models of patterns in human-produced data. They can be useful companions, but they are not a final gate for truth.



What they tend to do

produce plausible common answers
average across many writing patterns
compress complicated claims into fluent language
sound confident even when the source is weak



Why they are still useful

they can expose hidden assumptions
they can draft small workflow components
they can search the shape of an ill-defined relation
they can help when human experience is hard to model directly



The skill is not “believe or reject AI.” The skill is using it, then deciding what kind of check must happen before the output becomes evidence.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: The useful part is also the dangerous part
text:
The useful part is also the dangerous part

Common answer problem Because LLMs learn from pooled writing, they often produce the most available or average explanation. That can be helpful for orientation, but it can miss local constraints, updated facts, minority cases, and project-specific physics.


Design implication Do not ask only, “What does AI say?” Ask: what local fact, mechanism, calculation, or observed experience would push this answer away from the common mean?

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Not every AI output needs the same check
text:
Not every AI output needs the same check








AI output type
What it is good for
Final-gate check




Fact-based reiteration
summarize standards, definitions, precedent claims, code-like information
verify against primary source, datasheet, standard, or cited document


Relationship-based simulation
reason about fuzzy links: comfort, perception, spatial experience, thermal/acoustic sensation
compare with engineering/science logic, empirical evidence, sensitivity test, or bounded calculation


Workflow/code drafting
produce formulas, scripts, GhPython snippets, notebook cells, checklists
run it, inspect units/ranges, test known cases, and log failures




Final gate AI can help generate an answer. You decide which gate it must pass before it enters the design argument.

title: Week 8: Reproducibility and AI Fact-Checking
section: Human experience is messy enough that AI can help
text:
Human experience is messy enough that AI can help
Architecture often asks about relationships that are real but hard to reduce cleanly:

spatial atmosphere and perceived calm
thermal acceptability rather than just air temperature
acoustic comfort rather than only decibels
wayfinding confidence rather than only shortest path
facade perception rather than only performance values


A productive use AI can help generate hypotheses for these fuzzy relationships. It cannot validate them. Validation still comes from source checks, simple calculations, field observations, precedent mechanisms, simulations, or sensitivity tests.

The line is rarely “AI or not.” It is what kind of output is this, and what would make it trustworthy enough to use?

The artifact A building-performance analysis: polished charts, statistics beyond the author’s stated skill, no understanding of the method when questioned, no disclosure of AI use.

which claims are factual, which are relationship-based, and which are workflow/code?

what should have been disclosed, and where?
what is the minimum honest version of this output?


We critique the workflow and its claims, never the author’s ability.

AI can draft the step. It cannot be the final gate for its own output. That gate is your responsibility, every time.

“What implementation barriers am I likely missing?”

title: Week 4: GIS Choices for Architects
text:
1930s: redlining maps that shaped cities





HOLC “residential security” map, Brooklyn, 1930s. Public domain / CC BY-SA, via Wikimedia Commons.

You learn most by examining the reasoning inside work you have already done — not by adding new work. Every week, the same four questions, pointed at that week’s object:


Did What did I actually do, step by step?


Assumed What did I assume at each step?


Risk Where did I not check — where could it break?


Verify What would I verify if I did it again?


The point is not to judge old work. It is to see how its argument was built.

Evidence needs a workflow

precedent images can be useful, but rarely prove performance on their own
simulation numbers can be precise, but still depend on assumptions
survey comments can be rich, but need context before they generalize
data only becomes useful when the path from input to decision is legible


A finding is evidence only when someone else can inspect how you got it.

title: Week 1: Why Evidence Needs a Workflow

Sometimes evidence is just vibes


A vibe is not useless It is often the first clue that something might matter.


A vibe is not enough by itself It gets stronger only when the next step asks what would confirm, qualify, or challenge it.


For each image next: name the vibe claim, what it does not show yet, and the next evidence move.

section: 2012: a copy-paste error inside a risk model
text:
2012: a copy-paste error inside a risk model

What happened JPMorgan’s “London Whale” risk model lived in a chain of spreadsheets where values were copied and pasted between cells by hand. One step divided by a sum instead of an average, understating the risk. The losses reached about US$6 billion.


The lesson A spreadsheet is a transparent comparison layer only if its steps are inspectable. Manual copy-paste between cells is exactly where the logic stops being traceable.

GIS In layers + CRS · Varies operation sequence · Out spatial comparison · Check CRS stated, counts spot-checked


Python / notebook In data files + paths · Varies analysis parameters · Out figure / table · Check runs top-to-bottom, paths stated




GH / parametric In geometry + sliders · Varies the design space · Out comparable variants · Check variants share assumptions


BIM/BEM / simulation In model + settings · Varies scenario assumptions · Out performance result · Check dominant assumptions documented


AI-assisted In prompt + source data · Varies what AI generates / edits · Out drafted component · Check a manual review confirms it



Pick the route that makes your decision more defensible — not the one that looks most impressive.

You will use AI — so use it accountably
Four obligations that travel with any AI-assisted work — this is ML Primer Principle 12 in practice:


Disclose State what AI did, the prompts/seeds, and what you verified. Undisclosed AI is the problem, not AI use.


Sources & IP Use open or owned references; cite image and data sources; respect licenses; do not pass a model’s averaged answer off as your own evidence.

Accountability You remain responsible for every claim. AI is a companion, never the final gate — and never identify people without consent.

1986: the chart that did not show the danger

What went wrong The night before the Challenger launch, engineers argued against a cold-weather launch — but their charts scattered O-ring damage across thirteen pages and never plotted damage against temperature. The pattern stayed invisible; the launch was approved.


The lesson Correct data is not enough. If the figure does not make the relationship visible, the decision does not get made. (Edward Tufte’s classic case study of this launch.)

title: Week 9: Storytelling, Figures, and Decisions

Object-card anatomy
The whole card is built around one dominant recommendation. Everything else supports it.


1 · The dominant recommendation The one sentence the viewer must leave with. Largest, first, unmissable.


2 · One comparison figure A single legible chart that shows the comparison behind the recommendation — secondary to the headline, never competing with it.




3 · One threshold sentence The rule that turns the comparison into a decision: “we prefer X once the gain clears Y.”


4 · One limitations note Where the evidence is weakest and what would change the conclusion — small, honest, present.

The ML Workflow





graph LR

    B --> C[Split: Train/Test]

title: From ML Theory to Python Practice

Overfitting: The Villain




Too Simple: Misses patterns (underfitting)
Just Right: Captures true relationships
Too Complex: Memorizes noise (overfitting)



Solution: Cross-validation + hold-out test set

title: From ML Theory to Python Practice
text:
Cross-Validation in 30 Seconds


Problem: You don’t want to waste data on a single validation split
Solution: Split data into K “folds”, train K times, average the results
Benefit: More robust estimate of model performance
Standard: 5-fold or 10-fold CV






K-fold CV: Each fold gets to be the test set once

title: Python + ML Basics for Architects
text:
A fast, friendly introduction to Python, data handling, and simple machine learning — using fake but architecture-flavored data.
Goals: - Learn Python + pandas basics - Load and explore a dataset about windows/daylight/energy - Split into train/test, fit simple models, and evaluate - Understand cross-validation and overfitting with visuals - Get a small taste of neural nets via an MLP (“deep learning vibe”)


If you are on a fresh environment, you may need to install packages (run one by one if needed):
# !pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn scipy wordcloud
This notebook expects the repository structure with a data/ and scripts/ folder.

from pathlib import Path
import sys, warnings

# Add repo root and scripts to import path when running from notebooks/
if '__file__' in globals():
    ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
else:
    candidate = Path.cwd()
    if (candidate / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate
    elif candidate.name == 'notebooks' and (candidate.parent / 'scripts').exists():
        ROOT = candidate.parent
    else:
        ROOT = candidate
if str(ROOT / 'scripts') not in sys.path:
    sys.path.append(str(ROOT / 'scripts'))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

from plotting_utils import set_style, plot_cv_folds, confusion_matrix_plot, learning_curve_plot, validation_curve_plot
import data_simulation as sim

set_style()
np.random.seed(42)




Python stores numbers, strings, lists, and dictionaries. You’ll mostly use lists/dicts and then pandas DataFrames.

# Lists and dicts
sizes = [10, 20, 30]
room = {"name": "Studio A", "area_m2": 120, "seats": 40}
sizes.append(40)
{"sizes": sizes, "room": room}


# Numpy and pandas basics
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
a = np.array([1,2,3])
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1,2,3], "y": [3,2,1]})
df.describe()




We use fake data that mimics window-to-wall ratio (wwr), shading depth, orientation, and energy/daylight outcomes.

data_path = ROOT / 'data' / 'building_performance_fake.csv'
if not data_path.exists():
    # Generate defaults if missing
    sim.save_default_fake_data(ROOT)

df = pd.read_csv(data_path)
df.head()


df.describe(include='all')


sns.pairplot(df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','daylit_area','glare_probability','cooling_kwh_m2']])
plt.suptitle('Quick relationships', y=1.02);




We fit a simple linear model and evaluate on a held-out test set.

features = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation','glazing_u_w_m2k']
target = 'cooling_kwh_m2'
X = df[features]
y = df[target]

cat = ['orientation']
num = ['wwr','shading_depth_m','glazing_u_w_m2k']
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), cat),
    ("num", 'passthrough', num)
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
reg = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('model', LinearRegression())])
reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = reg.predict(X_test)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred)
r2, mae


plt.scatter(y_test, pred, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel('Actual cooling kWh/m²')
plt.ylabel('Predicted')
plt.title(f'Linear Regression: R²={r2:.2f}, MAE={mae:.1f}')
m = np.array([y_test.min(), y_test.max()])
plt.plot(m, m, 'k--', alpha=0.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Define a simple label: comfortable if glare_probability < 0.35 and daylit_area > 0.5.

df['comfortable'] = ((df['glare_probability'] < 0.35) & (df['daylit_area'] > 0.5)).astype(int)
Xc = df[['wwr','shading_depth_m','orientation']]
yc = df['comfortable']
pre_c = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['orientation']),
    ("num", 'passthrough', ['wwr','shading_depth_m'])
])
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=yc)
clf = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
clf.fit(Xtr, ytr)
predc = clf.predict(Xte)
acc = accuracy_score(yte, predc)
cm = confusion_matrix(yte, predc)
acc, cm


confusion_matrix_plot(cm, class_names=("Not Comfortable","Comfortable"), title=f'Logistic Regression (Accuracy={acc:.2f})');




We vary model complexity (polynomial degree) and show CV scores.

deg_scores = []
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for deg in range(1,7):
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=deg, include_bias=False)
    pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('poly', poly), ('ridge', Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
    deg_scores.append((deg, scores.mean(), scores.std()))

ds = pd.DataFrame(deg_scores, columns=['degree','cv_mean','cv_std'])
plt.errorbar(ds['degree'], ds['cv_mean'], yerr=ds['cv_std'], fmt='o-')
plt.xlabel('Polynomial degree (complexity)')
plt.ylabel('CV R²')
plt.title('Overfitting demo: watch CV score peak then drop')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
ds



Each row is a fold; green cells are train, red cells are test.

cv2 = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=7)
_ = plot_cv_folds(n_samples=len(X), cv_splits=cv2.split(np.arange(len(X))), title='5-fold CV: train vs test membership')
plt.show()





A small neural network classifier. This is just to build intuition — it’s not magic, and simple models are often enough.

mlp = Pipeline([('pre', pre_c), ('mlp', MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(16,8), max_iter=1000, random_state=42))])
mlp.fit(Xtr, ytr)
acc_mlp = accuracy_score(yte, mlp.predict(Xte))
acc, acc_mlp



How performance improves with more data.

_ = learning_curve_plot(clf, Xc, yc, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
plt.show()






Always hold out test data or use cross-validation
Start simple; only add complexity if it improves validated performance
Document random seeds and settings for reproducibility
“Deep” models need more data and care; don’t overfit
